parts: Please look at the files within /shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/height_adapted_zero_detection/, and consider the best research directions to pursue within this program
I’ll read the notes, trace their main claims and open problems, and compare the most promising directions for making progress.

The notes establish a useful detector coefficient, but the main gap is still cancellation in the full zero sum: a large coefficient alone does not force a measurable response. I’m focusing on a finite-interval detection theorem and the arithmetic costs needed to use it. I also found a newer classical zero-free-region input that should be included in the comparison.

Two useful refinements are emerging. Factoring out the height oscillation leaves a smoothly varying amplitude, which may reduce the cost of spectral truncation. Separately, the integer-only Hardy approximation route appears to have a concrete obstruction at large carrier heights. I’m checking both and will save a prioritized assessment in the investigation’s notes folder.

I’m using the write-page skill to save the assessment as a local research note, following the repository’s conventions. It will distinguish proved deductions from proposed work and leave the existing notes intact.

My current recommendation is to develop Gaussian localization and a carrier-centered arithmetic formula in parallel. The detector coefficients have more structure than the notes currently use: across the unit box, a fixed rotation puts them all in the same half-plane. That helps control a finite cluster, though the contribution from zeros outside the box still needs a bound.

The assessment has passed internal checks of the detector, arithmetic, and approximation arguments. It includes three useful deductions: a common-sector coefficient bound, a finite-cluster interval bound, and an approximation floor that rules out the natural integer-only shifted Hardy certificate in the current unit-box range. I’m saving it with the remaining gaps stated explicitly.

I recommend **a quantitative Gaussian-localized detector, developed alongside a carrier-centered arithmetic reduction**. This offers the clearest path from the existing coefficient lemmas to a usable zero-exclusion theorem.

After reading all three files and the linked investigations, I would prioritize:

1. **Complete the finite-interval detector.** Specify the continuous interval in \(\log X\), cluster loss, guard band, and every remainder. A useful additional deduction is that the detector coefficients occupy a common phase sector:
   \[
   \Re[-i\,\operatorname{sgn}(t)D_t(\rho)]>1/8
   \]
   throughout the existing unit box. This yields a separation-free lower bound for a finite cluster. Gaussian localization is the promising next step for controlling the remaining zeros.

2. **Rebuild the arithmetic formula around the carrier frequency.** Exact demodulation gives
   \[
   \ell_t(u)=u^{-it}L_t(u),
   \]
   with uniformly controlled amplitude derivatives. Centering the spectral truncation at \(t\) may therefore substantially reduce its cost. Begin with all von Mangoldt terms and the full divisor band; optional prime-power deletion already introduces restrictive losses near the current detector boundary.

3. **Update the classical calibration before choosing targets.** The March 2026 [Bellotti–Trudgian–Yang paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.21490v1) supplies the region \(\sigma>1-1/(4.896\log t)\). Also account for [rigorously verified RH through \(3\times10^{12}\)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09765). Finite boxes below that height are useful validation cases; a new exclusion result must extend beyond its input information.

4. **Keep alternative branches bounded.** Several nearby probes need explicit tests against positive-multiplicity clusters that nearly cancel on short, late intervals. For Hardy approximation, the natural integer-only shifted target has a concrete obstruction: its error exceeds \(0.896\) for \(|t|\ge100\), while the current unit-box certificate requires an error below \(0.5\). Real dilations or a different target deserve investigation. Large values need a new amplification mechanism before further investment.

The central unresolved issue remains an **independent bound for the complete signed arithmetic observable that beats the calibrated detector threshold**. The reductions alone do not supply that cancellation.
